```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

Reading about item response theory is one thing; deciding what to do with a
real test is another. The mirtverse labs put students in the analyst's chair.
Each lab is an interactive [learnr](https://rstudio.github.io/learnr/)
tutorial that runs in the browser. Students write and run live mirt code, look
at the results, and make the calls a working psychometrician makes. Every
decision gets immediate feedback that explains why the choice holds up or
doesn't.

The first part of this page is for students. Instructors will find a guide
and, at the very end, the [answer key](#answer-key).

## Start a lab in three steps

```{r}
install.packages("learnr")   # 1. once, if you don't have it
library(mirtverse)           # 2. load mirtverse
run_lab("model-choice")      # 3. open Lab 1 in your browser
```

`list_labs()` shows every lab with a short description. In RStudio, the labs
also appear in the **Tutorial** pane. Your progress is saved on your computer,
so you can close the lab and pick up where you left off.

## The labs

### Labs 1 and 2: the certification exam

You are the new psychometrician for the fictional **Northfield Certification
Board**. Its 32-item, five-option exam was taken by 1,200 candidates in
English or French, and the board wants to move from number-correct to IRT
scoring. The data (`certexam`) were simulated, so the truth is known, and a
few realistic problems are hidden in them for you to find.

| Lab | Run it with | You will |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Choosing a model the board can defend** (about 75 minutes) | `run_lab("model-choice")` | Score the responses, find a miskeyed item, check dimensionality, compare the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models, check fit and local dependence, and justify your choice |
| **2. From parameters to decisions** (about 75 minutes) | `run_lab("decisions")` | Read the item parameters, check precision at the pass mark, choose a scoring method, estimate how many candidates are misclassified, test for DIF between languages, write a memo to the board, and see the truth behind the data |

Lab 2 fits its own model at the start, so it can be done on its own.

### Lab 3: is the test fair?

You work for the fictional **Westvale Ministry of Education**. A parent group
says the Grade 6 numeracy test is biased against English language learners
(ELL), who scored three and a half points lower than their classmates. The
data (`numeracy`) cover 2,000 students, 500 of them ELL, on 30 items, and
`numeracy_items` describes each item.

| Lab | Run it with | You will |
|---|---|---|
| **3. Is the test fair? Detecting DIF** (about 75 minutes) | `run_lab("fairness")` | Separate a real group difference from item bias, run Mantel-Haenszel and IRT likelihood-ratio DIF tests, choose clean anchor items, judge how much the DIF matters for students' scores, plan a content review, and see the truth behind the data |

Lab 3 has its own storyline, so it can be done before or after Labs 1 and 2.

## What it looks like

Each section mixes short explanations, code exercises with hints and
solutions, and decision questions. A wrong answer becomes a teaching moment:

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(src = knitr::image_uri("figures/lab-screening.png"), width = "100%",
               alt = "Screening the items in Lab 1: the miskeyed item stands out, and choosing to drop it gets an explanation.")
```

At the end of each lab, you get a table of every decision you made, which you
can hand in as an assignment.

## For instructors

Labs 1 and 2 follow one storyline, but Lab 2 also works on its own; Lab 3
stands alone. The tables below list what students do in each section and the decisions they make. The
answers are in the [answer key](#answer-key) at the end of the page.
For where the labs fit in a full term, see the
[course map](course-map.html), a suggested 12-week syllabus.

### Lab 1: Choosing a model the board can defend

`run_lab("model-choice")`, about 75 minutes.

| Section | Students do | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| The brief | Meet the board and the raw data | |
| Score the responses | `key2binary()` | Why score before fitting? |
| Screen the items | Proportion correct, corrected item-total correlations and a distractor analysis | What to do with a suspicious item |
| How many dimensions? | One- vs two-factor 2PL, `anova()`, rotated loadings | Is one dimension defensible? |
| Compare the models | `select_model()` on Rasch, 2PL, 3PL | Which model to recommend |
| Check the chosen model | `gg_itemfit()`, `gg_q3()` | How to treat flagged item fit and local dependence |
| Commit to a model | Fit `final`, write a justification | Free-text justification, then a model answer |
| Your decisions | A table of every answer the student gave | |

### Lab 2: From parameters to decisions

`run_lab("decisions")`, about 75 minutes. The board's 2PL model is fitted in
the lab's setup, so students can start Lab 2 without finishing Lab 1.

| Section | Students do | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Read the items | `coef(IRTpars = TRUE)`, `gg_trace()` | Which item is hardest and what its low slope means; reading a trace line |
| Precision at the pass mark | Map the raw cut of 18 to theta with the EAP sum-score table; `gg_info()`, `testinfo()` | Is the exam precise enough at the cut, and what items would help? |
| Choose a scoring method | Compare EAP, ML and sum-score scale scores | What goes on candidates' score reports |
| Classification accuracy | Misclassification probabilities from each candidate's score and SE | How to respond to measurement error near the cut |
| Fairness across languages | Raw means by group, `dif()`, `gg_dif()` | Impact versus DIF; what to do with the flagged items |
| The memo | Free-text memo, then `interpret()` and `item_card()` | |
| The reveal | `lab_truth()`, true versus estimated difficulties | Where the 2PL departs from the true 3PL |

### Lab 3: Is the test fair? Detecting DIF

`run_lab("fairness")`, about 75 minutes. Three exercises fit 31 models each
and take about a minute; the lab warns students before each one.

| Section | Students do | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| The brief | Meet the complaint, `numeracy` and `numeracy_items` | |
| Impact or bias? | Proportion correct by group for every item | What a raw group difference shows |
| Match on the total score | Mantel-Haenszel by hand for one item, then ETS A/B/C categories for all | What DIF that favours the focal group means |
| The IRT approach | `dif()`, `gg_dif(type = "curves")` | Why IRT flags an item that Mantel-Haenszel misses |
| Choose clean anchors | A multiple-group model with only unflagged items as anchors; `DIF(scheme = "add")` | Which impact estimate to report; which flags were artefacts |
| How much does it matter? | Differential test functioning from the expected test score curves, and each item's share | What to tell the deputy minister |
| Content review | Join the flagged items to the item descriptions | What the review panel should do |
| The memo | Free-text memo, then `interpret()` | |
| The reveal | `lab_truth("numeracy")`, then a gender DIF analysis | Reporting a null result |

### Tips for running the labs

* **Before class:** ask students to install mirtverse and learnr and run
  `list_labs()`. Fitting the models needs no internet connection.
* **Order:** Labs 1 and 2 belong together. Lab 3 works on its own and fits a
  unit on fairness or validity; Lab 2's short DIF section is a good warm-up
  for it.
* **Speed:** most exercises run in under about 15 seconds on a laptop; the
  two-factor model uses fewer quadrature points so it stays quick. The full
  DIF analyses in Labs 2 and 3 take up to a minute.
* **Hosting:** to run a lab in the browser without any installation, deploy
  the tutorial folder (`system.file("tutorials", "model-choice", package =
  "mirtverse")`) to shinyapps.io or Posit Connect. learnr's event recorder
  (`options(tutorial.event_recorder = ...)`) can log students' answers there.
* **Assessment:** the free-text justification at the end of each lab makes a
  good short assignment. Ask students to paste it, together with their
  decision table, into your course site.

## Answer key

This section gives the answers away.

### The planted problems

`certexam` is simulated from item parameters based on a 3PL
calibration of mirt's `SAT12` data, so the items behave like real ones. Because
the data were generated, the truth is known, and a few problems were planted
on purpose:

| Planted problem | Where students meet it | What a good analyst does |
|---|---|---|
| Q14 is miskeyed in `certexam_key` | Lab 1, item screening | Spots the negative item-total correlation, checks the key with a distractor analysis, fixes it and rescores |
| Q21 and Q22 share a reading passage | Lab 1, dimensionality and local dependence | Recognises a two-item "factor" as local dependence, not a second trait; treats the pair as a testlet |
| Guessing on harder items (the true model is the 3PL) | Lab 1, model comparison | Weighs AIC against BIC, convergence and sample size; 2PL and 3PL are both defensible, Rasch is not |
| Q09 (uniform) and Q27 (non-uniform) show DIF against French candidates | Lab 2, fairness | Flags both for content review |
| French candidates score 0.35 SD lower on average | Lab 2, fairness | Separates a real group difference (impact) from DIF |

`lab_truth()` returns the generating values for instructors.

### Lab 1

* **Why score first:** the 2PL and 3PL model the probability of a correct
  answer.
* **Negative item-total correlation:** check the key before anything else.
* **Real key for Q14:** A. About 90% of the top 20% of candidates chose it;
  the published key says C.
* **Dimensions:** one. The likelihood-ratio test and AIC favour two factors,
  BIC favours one, and the second factor is made only of Q21 and Q22.
* **Model:** the 2PL (lowest BIC, converges, M2 RMSEA about 0.015) or the 3PL
  (lowest AIC, but it does not converge with default settings and its guessing
  parameters are poorly determined at N = 1,200). Both are accepted; the
  feedback names the trade-off. Rasch is rejected by every criterion.
* **Item fit:** a couple of items have p < .01, but after a
  false-discovery-rate correction none is flagged at that level, and the
  misfit is small (RMSEA about 0.03).
* **Q21 and Q22:** Q3 of about 0.27, more than twice any other pair. Combine
  them into a testlet score, model the passage, or keep one item; at minimum,
  report it.

#### Discussion prompts

* The likelihood-ratio test rejected one dimension. Why is that not enough to
  conclude the exam measures two traits?
* The true model is the 3PL, yet BIC prefers the 2PL. Is BIC "wrong"? What is
  model selection trying to find?
* A candidate who failed by one point appeals. Which parts of your analysis
  would you want to show the appeal panel?

The decision table at the end of Lab 1, for a student who made these choices:

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(src = knitr::image_uri("figures/lab-decisions.png"), width = "100%",
               alt = "The decision table at the end of Lab 1.")
```

### Lab 2

* **Hardest item:** Q32 (b about 3), with Q12 close behind. Both have low
  slopes (about 0.45), the 2PL's way of absorbing guessing.
* **Trace line:** at theta = 0, Q32's probability is about 0.2.
* **Pass mark:** raw 18 corresponds to theta of about 0.05. Information there
  is about 6 (SE about 0.41), close to the exam's peak at theta of about -0.5.
  Medium-difficulty, highly discriminating items would help most.
* **Scoring:** scale scores from the sum-score table (every candidate with the
  same raw score gets the same score) are the most defensible for
  certification; pattern EAP is accepted with the caveat about explaining it.
  ML is undefined for perfect and zero scores.
* **Classification:** about 145 of 1,200 candidates (12%) are expected to be
  misclassified, and about 364 (30%) are within one SE of the cut. Report it,
  and consider a retest policy or more items near the cut; don't move the cut.
* **Impact:** French candidates are estimated 0.38 SD lower (true value
  0.35). That is a group difference, not item bias.
* **DIF:** only Q09 (uniform; about 15 percentage points harder for French
  candidates at the same ability) and Q27 (non-uniform; the curves cross) are
  flagged. Send both to bilingual content review.
* **Truth:** the 2PL departs most from the true difficulties for the hardest
  items, where guessing matters.

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(src = knitr::image_uri("figures/lab-dif.png"), width = "100%",
               alt = "DIF item curves by group in Lab 2: Q09 is uniformly harder for French candidates, Q27's curves cross.")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(src = knitr::image_uri("figures/lab-reveal.png"), width = "100%",
               alt = "The reveal: estimated 2PL difficulties against the true 3PL values. The hardest items, where guessing matters, depart most.")
```

#### Discussion prompts

* Two candidates both answered 18 items correctly. Under pattern scoring one
  passes and one fails. How would you explain that to them? Would you?
* Q27's average (signed) DIF effect is small. Why is that misleading?
* The board's 2PL was "wrong", yet most of the decisions it supported were
  right. When does using a simpler model than the truth matter?

### Lab 3

The planted problems in `numeracy` (`lab_truth("numeracy")` returns them):

| Planted problem | What a good analyst does |
|---|---|
| ELL students are 0.5 SD lower on average | Treats it as impact, not bias: the clean-anchor model estimates it at 0.55 SD |
| N07, N18, N20, N25 and N30, long word problems, are harder for ELL students at the same ability (uniform DIF) | Flags them with both methods and sends them to content review |
| N02, a word problem with an idiom, discriminates poorly for ELL students (non-uniform DIF) | Notices that Mantel-Haenszel misses it and the IRT test catches it |
| N21, a symbolic item, is easier for ELL students | Flags it for review too, rather than keeping it to offset the others |
| N03 has a tiny shift | Leaves it alone |
| N10, N12 and N28 are just as long as the DIF items but show no DIF | Concludes that length alone does not explain the DIF |
| No gender DIF and no gender impact | Reports the null result with the sample size |

* **Raw gaps:** ELL students do worse on 29 of 30 items (by up to 35
  percentage points on N30); only N21 goes the other way. That says nothing
  about bias yet.
* **Mantel-Haenszel:** D for N07 is about -2.2. Category C: N07, N20, N25 and
  N30 (negative) and N21 (positive, about +2.6). Category B: N18 and N15. N02
  is in category A, because its curves cross.
* **N21:** large DIF that favours ELL students. It needs review like the
  others.
* **First IRT pass (`dif()`):** ten items flagged: the seven planted ones plus
  N05, N15 and N16, which have small positive effects. N02's esd is near 0
  but its uesd is about 0.15: non-uniform DIF.
* **Clean anchor:** with the 20 unflagged items as anchors, the ELL mean moves
  from -0.68 to -0.55 SD (true value -0.5), and N05, N15 and N16 are no
  longer flagged. They were artefacts of a contaminated anchor.
* **How much it matters:** for an ELL and a fluent student of the same
  ability, the DIF costs the ELL student about 0.7 of a point out of 30. The
  five word problems cost about 0.8; N21 gives back about 0.2. Most of the
  3.5-point gap is impact. Cancellation does not make the items fair.
* **Content review:** send all seven items to a panel with ELL and numeracy
  specialists, and revise wording in plain language. Length alone is not the
  explanation, since N10, N12 and N28 are just as long. Field-test the
  revised items and check them for DIF again.
* **Gender:** no item is flagged and the means are almost equal. Report "no
  evidence of gender DIF" with the sample size; it is not proof of none.

```{r, echo = FALSE, eval = TRUE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(src = knitr::image_uri("figures/lab-fairness-curves.png"), width = "100%",
               alt = "Item curves by group in Lab 3: N07 is uniformly harder for ELL students, N21 is easier for them, and N02's curves cross.")
```

#### Discussion prompts

* Mantel-Haenszel and the IRT test disagreed about N02. When would you
  prefer each method?
* The first pass flagged three clean items. What would have happened if the
  ministry had removed every flagged item without a second pass?
* N21 favours ELL students and partly cancels the other DIF. Why is "it all
  balances out" not a good defence of a test?
* A plain-language revision of N07 is field-tested and still shows DIF. What
  would you look at next?
